title: VFR Cruising Altitudes, MEFs, and Glide Distance Planning

required_knowledge_points.title: NEODD/SWEVEN — 91.159 VFR Cruising Altitude Rule
required_knowledge_points.why: The DPE tests this with a cross: 'What altitude would you fly on a magnetic COURSE of 282°?' The trap is that the rule applies to magnetic COURSE (ground track), not magnetic HEADING. A pilot in a 30-knot crosswind may be heading 310° but tracking 282° — the altitude is determined by the 282° course.
required_knowledge_points.knowledge: 14 CFR 91.159 mandates specific cruising altitudes for VFR flight above 3,000 feet AGL. Magnetic COURSE 000° through 179° (NE quadrant) = ODD thousands + 500 feet (3,500 / 5,500 / 7,500 / 9,500). Magnetic COURSE 180° through 359° (SW quadrant) = EVEN thousands + 500 feet (4,500 / 6,500 / 8,500 / 10,500). Memory aid: NEODD / SWEVEN. Critical distinctions: (1) +500 feet is not optional — provides vertical separation from IFR aircraft at whole thousands. (2) Rule applies only ABOVE 3,000 feet AGL. (3) Based on magnetic COURSE (ground track), not magnetic HEADING (nose direction).
required_knowledge_points.knowledge_formatted:
### 14 CFR 91.159 — VFR Cruising Altitude Rule

| Magnetic COURSE | Quadrant | Altitude |
|---|---|---|
| **000° – 179°** | Northeast | **ODD thousands + 500 ft** (3,500 / 5,500 / 7,500 / 9,500) |
| **180° – 359°** | Southwest | **EVEN thousands + 500 ft** (4,500 / 6,500 / 8,500 / 10,500) |

**Memory Aid:** **NE**ODD / **SW**EVEN

### Three Critical Rules
1. The **+500 foot** suffix is **mandatory** — provides vertical separation from IFR aircraft at whole-thousand altitudes
2. Rule applies **only above 3,000 feet AGL** — no cruising altitude rule below 3,000 AGL
3. Based on magnetic **COURSE** (track over ground) — **NOT** magnetic **HEADING** (nose direction)

### Course vs. Heading — The DPE Trap
- In a 30-knot crosswind, heading and course can differ by **20°+**
- Magnetic COURSE 282° = Southwest quadrant → **EVEN + 500** (4,500, 6,500...)
- Even if the **heading** is 305° (NE quadrant) — the **course** governs

required_knowledge_points.title: Maximum Elevation Figures (MEF) — What They Are and What They Are NOT
required_knowledge_points.why: The most dangerous misread of a sectional chart: a pilot sees MEF 4,300 on a quadrant and cruises at 4,500, thinking that provides 200 feet of clearance. The FAA adds only 100 feet above the highest obstacle for the MEF value. This is a CFIT trap.
required_knowledge_points.knowledge: Maximum Elevation Figures (MEFs) appear in blue on sectional charts inside each latitude/longitude quadrant. MEF = the highest elevation of terrain or obstacle within that quadrant + 100 feet buffer (rounded up to next 100 foot increment). An MEF of 4,300 does NOT guarantee 200 feet of clearance if you fly at 4,500 — the 100-foot buffer may sit only 200 feet above an obstacle that was 4,377 feet. The safe altitude standard: 1,000 feet above MEF in non-congested areas and 2,000 feet above MEF in mountainous terrain per 14 CFR 91.119. Key: MEF = documentation of highest known obstacle with minimum buffer. Use it as a reference floor, not a cruising altitude guide.
required_knowledge_points.knowledge_formatted:
### Maximum Elevation Figure (MEF)
- Appears in **large blue numbers** inside each **1° latitude × 1° longitude** quadrant on the sectional chart
- Represents the **highest terrain or obstacle** in the quadrant + **100-foot buffer** (rounded up to the next 100 ft)

### What MEF Does NOT Guarantee
- MEF 4,300 does **not** mean 200 feet of clearance at 4,500 feet
- The 100-foot buffer is the **minimum margin** above the highest known obstacle
- Does not account for **undocumented obstacles** or recently erected structures

### Safe Altitude Standard (14 CFR 91.119)
| Terrain Type | Minimum Clearance Above MEF |
|---|---|
| Non-congested areas | **1,000 feet** above highest obstacle |
| Mountainous terrain | **2,000 feet** above terrain |

> **MEF = reference floor, not a cruising altitude** — fly 1,000 feet above it, minimum

required_knowledge_points.title: Glide Distance Planning — The Engine-Out Footprint
required_knowledge_points.why: The DPE asks: 'If your engine failed right now, could you reach a suitable landing site?' This requires the pilot to know their aircraft's best glide ratio, translate it to distance at current altitude, and identify suitable terrain — a calculation that must be done mentally and updated throughout the flight.
required_knowledge_points.knowledge: At best glide speed (Vg), the aircraft travels a predictable horizontal distance for every foot of altitude lost. Best glide ratio for most training aircraft (C172, PA-28): approximately 8:1 to 10:1. Quick estimate (10:1 ratio): 1,000 feet AGL = approximately 1.5 nm glide radius. 4,000 feet AGL = approximately 6 nm glide radius. Practical formula: altitude (feet) ÷ glide ratio = horizontal distance (feet), then ÷ 6,076 for nautical miles. Higher cruising altitude extends the engine-out footprint — the most effective risk mitigation for force-landing exposure over hazardous terrain.
required_knowledge_points.knowledge_formatted:
### Glide Ratio Basics
- At **best glide speed (Vg)**, the aircraft travels a predictable **horizontal distance for every foot of altitude lost**
- Best glide ratio for most training aircraft (C172, PA-28): **8:1 to 10:1**

### Glide Footprint — Quick Reference Table (using 10:1 ratio)
| Altitude AGL | Approx. Glide Radius |
|---|---|
| 1,000 ft | ~1.5 nm |
| 2,000 ft | ~3 nm |
| 4,000 ft | ~6 nm |
| 8,000 ft | ~12 nm |

### Formula (Precise Calculation)
- Horizontal distance (ft) = **altitude (ft) ÷ glide ratio**
- Convert to NM: horizontal distance (ft) **÷ 6,076**

### Why Altitude Matters
- Higher altitude = larger engine-out footprint = more emergency landing options
- Over terrain with no suitable surfaces for 10+ miles: **climb higher** as the primary risk mitigation
- Always mentally answer the question: **"Could I reach a useable surface from here if the engine quit right now?"**

required_knowledge_points.title: Wind vs. Altitude — The Performance vs. Safety Trade-Off
required_knowledge_points.why: An applicant who always selects the highest legal altitude demonstrates superficial knowledge. The DPE wants to see that the pilot evaluates actual Winds Aloft and makes a reasoned altitude choice balancing regulatory compliance, terrain clearance, glide footprint, and groundspeed efficiency.
required_knowledge_points.knowledge: Altitude selection involves four competing factors: (1) Regulatory: must comply with 91.159 cruising altitude values above 3,000 AGL. (2) Safety floor: must provide at least 1,000 feet clearance above terrain per 91.119. (3) Performance: if a strong headwind exists at high altitude vs. a tailwind at low altitude, the low altitude may yield better groundspeed and fuel efficiency. (4) Emergency footprint: higher altitude extends the engine-out glide radius. Framework: check Winds Aloft at multiple levels (6,000, 9,000, 12,000 feet). If the headwind at 9,500 is 25 knots stronger than at 5,500, the lower altitude may provide better groundspeed while still meeting terrain clearance.
required_knowledge_points.knowledge_formatted:
### Four Competing Factors in Altitude Selection

| Factor | Regulation | What It Requires |
|---|---|---|
| **Regulatory** | 14 CFR 91.159 | Comply with NEODD/SWEVEN above 3,000 AGL |
| **Safety floor** | 14 CFR 91.119 | 1,000 ft above obstacles (non-congested), 2,000 ft over mountains |
| **Performance** | 14 CFR 91.103 | Evaluate Winds Aloft — headwinds and TAS at each level |
| **Emergency footprint** | Best judgment | Higher altitude = larger glide radius if engine fails |

### Wind vs. Altitude Decision Framework
1. Obtain **Winds Aloft** at multiple levels (6,000 / 9,000 / 12,000 ft) for the route
2. Calculate **effective groundspeed** at each candidate altitude (TAS ± wind)
3. Verify **terrain clearance** (at least 1,000 ft above MEF)
4. Evaluate **emergency footprint** (adequate landing options within glide distance?)

### Bottom Line
- If a 25-knot stronger headwind at 9,500 makes 5,500 the better velocity choice AND terrain clearance is met → select **5,500**
- If you're crossing hazardous no-landing terrain → the **emergency footprint** argument may override wind efficiency
- **High is not always better** — reasoning through the four factors is the correct answer

lesson_overview:
## VFR Cruising Altitudes, MEFs, and Glide Distance — Altitude Is a Decision, Not a Default

Most student pilots pick their cruising altitude the way they pick a lane on the highway — habit or convenience. A professional pilot uses altitude as an active tool. The right altitude manages terrain clearance, regulatory compliance, engine-out survivability, and wind efficiency simultaneously. This lesson teaches you how to think about altitude before every flight — not just what the rule says.

**91.159: NEODD/SWEVEN — the rule and the trap.** Any VFR flight above 3,000 feet AGL must comply with flight-level altitude assignments based on magnetic COURSE. Northeast quadrant (000 through 179 degrees): odd thousands plus 500 feet (3,500, 5,500, 7,500...). Southwest quadrant (180 through 359 degrees): even thousands plus 500 feet (4,500, 6,500, 8,500...). The plus-500 is mandatory — not optional. It creates vertical separation between VFR traffic (at the half-thousands) and IFR traffic (at the whole thousands). The trap that catches checkride applicants: the rule uses magnetic COURSE — the track your aircraft makes over the ground — not magnetic HEADING. In a 30-knot crosswind, your heading and course can differ by 20+ degrees. A track of 185 degrees is a southwest course — EVEN plus 500 — even if the nose is pointed at 205 degrees.

**Below 3,000 AGL: no cruising altitude rule.** 91.159 does not apply below 3,000 feet AGL. In the low-altitude environment — training areas, pattern work, sightseeing below 3,000 feet — you are not legally required to hold a specific altitude tier. But 91.119 minimum safe altitude requirements still apply regardless.

**MEFs: what they are and what they are NOT.** Maximum Elevation Figures appear in large blue numbers inside each one-degree latitude/longitude quadrant on the sectional chart. Each MEF represents the highest terrain or obstacle in that quadrant PLUS a 100-foot buffer (rounded up to the next 100-foot increment). MEF 4,300 means the highest known obstacle is approximately 4,200 feet or less — with only 100 feet of buffer above it. If you cruise at 4,500 feet you have as little as 200 feet of clearance — and zero allowance for undocumented obstacles, survey errors, or recently erected towers. The professional standard: maintain at least 1,000 feet above MEF over non-congested areas, and 2,000 feet above terrain in mountainous regions. Never use MEF as a cruising altitude floor.

**Glide distance: the silent argument for altitude.** Every foot of altitude you carry is a potential foot-forward in an engine failure. Your aircraft's best glide ratio — typically 8:1 to 10:1 for most training aircraft — means you travel 8 to 10 feet forward for every foot of altitude lost at Vg. Quick estimate: 1,000 feet AGL gives you roughly 1.3 to 1.5 nautical miles of glide radius. 8,000 feet AGL: approximately 10-12 nautical miles. Before every cross-country, know your glide footprint at your current altitude and be able to identify at least one suitable emergency landing area within that radius.

**The checkride trap:** The DPE gives you a magnetic COURSE of 282 degrees and asks for a legal cruising altitude. Students who immediately say '4,500 or 6,500' have answered partially — but the DPE is watching to see if you catch the COURSE vs HEADING distinction. 282 degrees is southwest quadrant — EVEN plus 500 — so 4,500, 6,500, etc. Then: 'How did you determine that was your course and not your heading?' That follow-up is the real test.
